$comment: AN EXISTING GRAPH THAT SHARES THE VOCABULARY BUT NONE OF THE FACTS.
WHY THIS SHAPE, AND WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT PROVE. Grounding is measured by giving the
extractor a graph and seeing whether it reuses that graph's predicates. Seeding it with the
octopus golden triples would be circular — handing over the answer key and then congratulating
the model for reading it. So every fact here is about a DIFFERENT species: cuttlefish, giant
squid, nautilus. Not one statement mentions the common octopus, and no object here appears in
What the predicates share is the RELATIONAL VOCABULARY — has-heart-count, is-found-in,
feeds-on, has-predator — because that is the real situation the feature exists for: a graph
that already describes things of this kind, meeting a document about a new one.
STATED PLAINLY SO THE RESULT IS NOT OVERSOLD: this measures 'if the graph already uses our
words, does the model reuse them?', which is the product scenario. It does NOT measure whether
a model can guess our vocabulary unaided — it cannot, and that is the whole point of F136.
Every predicate appears at least twice, deliberately: selectVocabulary drops predicates used
once (graph-lint's finding that 24% of predicate types are private one-offs), so a fixture with
singletons would silently offer the model nothing and read as a null result.
